title: Vue Rendering Architectures
keywords: Selecting an architecture for an application
subtopics: Selecting an architecture for an application
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Vue Rendering Architectures in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Vue Rendering Architectures within Server-Side Rendering, Nuxt, and Deployment. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Rendering choices affect initial content, hydration, deployment complexity, caching, security, and the availability of browser-only APIs.

content_blocks.title: Vue Rendering Architectures: Server rendering and hydration
content_blocks.alt_text: Server rendering and hydration diagram for lesson 135: Vue Rendering Architectures. Render deterministic HTML for this request → Send markup without shared mutable user state → Attach events to matching initial output
content_blocks.caption: Rendering flow: server output and client hydration must agree, and per-request state must remain isolated.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Vue rendering may be client-side, server-rendered, or pre-rendered; Nuxt provides an opinionated application framework for SSR/SSG use cases. This lesson focuses on Vue Rendering Architectures. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Client-side rendering (CSR)
items.text: For Client-side rendering (CSR), express the intended DOM result through a Vue template binding instead of directly manipulating the DOM. Keep template expressions small, use stable keys for stateful list items, and choose directives based on whether content should be created, removed, or merely hidden.

items.title: Server-side rendering (SSR)
items.text: For Server-side rendering (SSR), decide which code runs during build, on the server, and in the browser. Keep output deterministic during hydration, isolate state per server request, keep secrets server-only, and test the actual production build rather than relying only on the dev server.

items.title: Static-site generation (SSG)
items.text: For Static-site generation (SSG), connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Hydration
items.text: For Hydration, decide which code runs during build, on the server, and in the browser. Keep output deterministic during hydration, isolate state per server request, keep secrets server-only, and test the actual production build rather than relying only on the dev server.

items.title: Selecting an architecture for an application
items.text: For Selecting an architecture for an application, bind the input to a clear state value, validate before submission, and associate field errors with their controls. A disabled or loading state should be reflected in the UI without treating the client as the authority for server validation.

content_blocks.expected_output: The viewport width is read only in the browser after mount, avoiding a server-side reference to window.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use the snippet in a Vue SFC. Test server and browser behavior separately; if rendered state depends on time/randomness, ensure hydration output is deterministic.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Vue Rendering Architectures with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Server-side rendering (SSR)”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Vue rendering may be client-side, server-rendered, or pre-rendered; Nuxt provides an opinionated application framework for SSR/SSG use cases. For Vue Rendering Architectures, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Vue Rendering Architectures” that applies “Client-side rendering (CSR)”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Client-side rendering (CSR)”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Vue Rendering Architectures belongs to the broader area Server-Side Rendering, Nuxt, and Deployment.
The main concept to practice is Client-side rendering (CSR).
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
